3. Physiological relevance of Organoid Experiments
In Figures 3 and 4, the authors use intestinal organoids and show that volumetric
compression induces LLPS in stem cells. However, the physiological relevance of
globally compressing the entire organoid is unclear. The study aims to understand
how mechanical forces in the intestinal crypt influence cell fate. Organoids are
indeed a powerful system for this investigation. However, compressing the entire
organoid via PEG treatment affects all cells non-specifically and may not mimic
localized mechanical cues, such as compression from neighboring cells at the
crypt base.
A more physiologically relevant approach might involve applying localized pressure to specific cell populations (e.g., stem cells). The current method—immersing organoids in PEG—induces uniform volumetric compression, which may not accurately reflect the in vivo mechanical microenvironment.
Reply: We appreciate this important concern about the physiological relevance of
global organoid compression versus localized mechanical forces in native crypts.
This raises valid questions about experimental design that deserve careful
consideration.
We acknowledge that PEG-mediated compression affects all cells uniformly,
whereas in vivo mechanical forces may be spatially heterogeneous. However, we
respectfully argue two aspect: first, the osmolarity in intestinal microenvironment
indeed varied globally during digestion cycles and water adsorption; second, our
approach captures the essential downstream physical consequence from diverse
mechanical inputs in native tissue, the decreased cell volume and increased
intracellular macromolecular crowding.
Several lines of evidence support the physiological relevance of our approach.
First, our in vivo measurements (Li et al., Cell Stem Cell, 2021) demonstrate that
volumes (200-300 μm³) compared to differentiated cells in less crowded regions
(400-600 μm³), with deformed nuclear morphology indicating spatial constraint.
ISCs exhibited a large cell volume expansion (7-8 folds) immediately after isolated
from native tissue to matrigel 3D culturing. The PEG concentrations we employed
(1-3%) produce volume reductions of 23-38% in cultured cells and organoids, well
within this physiologically observed range.
Second, intestinal epithelial cells naturally experience significant osmotic
variations that cause volume changes throughout the day. Luminal osmolarity
varies cyclically during digestion cycles (300-500 mOsm), creating physiological
volume fluctuations that all epithelial cells must accommodate (Li Y, et al., Nature
Reviews Bioengineering, 2024, 2(12): 1023-1038.). Recent studies measured
osmolarity in mice intestine in a range between 300 mOsm and 1100 mOsm
(Tropini C, et al. Cell, 2018, 173(7): 1742-1754. e17; Ng K M, et al. MBio,
2023, 14(4): e00753-23.); another study measure gastrointestinal osmolarity in a
range of 300 to 900 mOsm in Rock Hyrax. The in vivo stimuli of physiological
relevant osmotic change in animal studies are widely using 500 mOsm and even
1500 mOsm (Ichiki T, et al. Nature, 2022, 602(7897): 468-474; Zimmerman C A,
et al. Nature, 2019, 568(7750): 98-102.). Our use of osmotic compression, with an
osmolarity of of 362.5 mOsm (+1% PEG 300) to 400 mOsm (+2% PEG 300), and
437.5 mOsm (+3% PEG 300), thus models a naturally occurring challenge rather
than an artificial perturbation in physiological relevant range. Furthermore, our
previous work demonstrated that multiple distinct mechanical inputs—3D hydrogel
compression, substrate stiffness variations, and biaxial stretch—all converge on
similar volumetric compression and produce comparable Wnt signaling responses
(Li et al., Cell Stem Cell, 2021, Figs. 2I-K). This suggests that volumetric
compression represents a common downstream integrator of diverse upstream
mechanical forces.
Third, we emphasize that our primary scientific question is: when cell volume
decreases and intracellular crowding increases, how do phase separation
mechanisms transduce this physical state into biochemical signaling outputs?
Global PEG compression provides a tractable experimental system to
systematically test this mechanism while maintaining cell viability and enabling
29
quantitative imaging of intracellular condensate dynamics.
We agree that future studies incorporating spatial heterogeneity would
strengthen the physiological relevance. Microfluidic devices enabling localized
compression of organoid subregions, or optogenetic approaches to spatially
control crowding, would be valuable extensions. However, we believe our current
approach successfully identifies the core mechanism (crowding-driven AXIN
phase separation bidirectionally regulates Wnt signaling) and demonstrates its
functional consequences in organoid systems. The consistency between our in
vitro observations and in vivo stem cell volume measurements supports the
physiological relevance of this mechanism.

4. Additional Concerns Regarding Experimental Results
4-1.Localization of AXIN LLPS in Organoids (Fig. 4):
While the authors show that volumetric compression induces LLPS of AXIN in
organoids, they do not identify the subcellular localization of these condensates.
Based on HEK293T experiments, LLPS occurs in the cytoplasm when Wnt
30
signaling is off, and at the plasma membrane when Wnt signaling is on (Figs. 1
and 2). The authors should investigate and report whether similar
compartmentalization occurs in different organoid cell types (e.g., stem cells vs.
Paneth cells).
Reply: We thank you for this comment. You query about the subcellular
localization of AXIN condensates in different organoid cell types. However, the
current technical challenge exists in performing simultaneous, multi-color live-cell
imaging to definitively distinguish AXIN condensate and their co-components
dynamics in specific cell types (e.g., stem cells, Paneth cells, and more) within the
same 3D organoid, due to limitations in robust, multiplexed cell-type-specific
fluorescent labeling systems.
Given this technical context, we strategically focused our investigation on the
cell populations where the AXIN-based mechanochemical circuit is theoretically
most critical and biologically relevant. For Wnt-OFF/bypassed model, it can only
happens in CRC organoids, since healthy intestinal organoids required Wnt
ligands to survival. And for CRC organoids, there is only colorectal cancer cells
existing, there is neither intestinal stem cells or Paneth cells. For Wnt-ON model,
even though there are stem cells or Paneth cells: the Paneth cells are terminally
differentiated cells; their following cell fate are not regulated by Wnt signaling
activation. Instead, the fate of intestinal stem cells (ISCs) are mastered by the Wnt
signaling activity. A high Wnt signaling leads to self-renewing of ISCs; a modulate
activation of Wnt signaling leads to differentiation of ISCs; and a depleted Wnt
signaling results in the death of ISCs. Thus, the function of this AXIN based
mechanochemical circuit is important in ISCs. For this reason, we imaged the
formation of AXIN condensates for Wnt-ON state in ISC organoids, which is a
formation of intestinal organoids with high purity of ISCs.
As a result, we have conducted fluorescence-based imaging assays in two
organoid models representing distinct Wnt signaling states:
1. Intestinal stem cell (ISC) organoids (Wnt-ON model):
These organoids are cultured in ISC medium with Wnt ligands and represent
a canonical Wnt-ON state. We observed that AXIN condensates showed
enrichment at the cell membrane under basal conditions. Following PEG
compression, AXIN condensates showed further enhanced membrane localization
31
(Fig. S5a and b), consistent with increased LRP6 signalosome formation.
2. Colorectal cancer (CRC) organoids (Wnt-OFF/bypassed model):
These organoids harbor APC mutations that disrupt the destruction complex.
We observed AXIN condensates colocalizing with APC in the cytoplasm. Following
PEG compression, the degree of AXIN-APC colocalization was further enhanced
(Fig. S5c and d), consistent with increased destruction complex assembly.
Overall, the results confirmed the subcellular localization of AXIN-based
condensates in different formats of organoid systems.

4-2. Physiological Relevance of Volume Reduction (Figs. 1 and 2):
The authors apply volumetric compression to HEK293T cells using PEG. However,
the extent of volume reduction used to mimic physiological pressure in the
intestinal crypt is not justified. If the reduction is outside physiological range, the
results may not be biologically meaningful, as elevated macromolecular
33
concentration alone can drive LLPS. The authors should estimate the physiological
volume reduction experienced in vivo and relate it to their experimental setup,
ideally referencing phase diagrams for AXIN condensates.
Reply: We thank you for this comment. The physiological relevance of volume
reduction is important to be included in this paper.
Intestinal epithelial cells naturally experience significant osmotic variations in
vivo. Studies have documented that luminal osmolarity in the intestine ranges from
approximately 300 to 450 mOsm during daily digestion and drinking (Li Y, et al.,
Nature Reviews Bioengineering, 2024, 2(12): 1023-1038.), creating a dynamic
osmotic environment that cells must continuously adapt to. Recent studies
measured osmolarity in mice intestine in a range between 300 mOsm and 1100
mOsm (Tropini C, et al. Cell, 2018, 173(7): 1742-1754. e17; Ng K M, et al. MBio,
2023, 14(4): e00753-23.); another study measure gastrointestinal osmolarity in a
range of 300 to 900 mOsm in Rock Hyrax. The in vivo stimuli of physiological
relevant osmotic change in animal studies are widely using 500 mOsm and even
1500 mOsm (Ichiki T, et al. Nature, 2022, 602(7897): 468-474; Zimmerman C A,
et al. Nature, 2019, 568(7750): 98-102.). This physiological osmotic variability
provides important context for understanding how cells in the intestinal epithelium
respond to volume changes and crowding. The osmolarity we employed in this
paper is roughly 362.5 mOsm (+1% PEG 300) to 400 mOsm (+2% PEG 300), and
437.5 mOsm (+3% PEG 300); all are within a physiologically-relevant range. Our
use of PEG 300 to induce osmotic compression thus models a naturally occurring
physical challenge that intestinal cells regularly encounter.
The PEG concentrations used in our experiments (1-2%) were carefully
calibrated to replicate physiologically relevant compression levels. In our previous
work (Li et al., Cell Stem Cell 2021), we quantified cell volumes in mouse intestinal
crypts and found that Lgr5+ stem cells at the crowded crypt base exhibit volumes
of ~200-300 μm³, while Lgr5− differentiated cells in less crowded regions show
volumes of ~400-600 μm³, representing approximately 50% volume reduction
under physiological crowding. To validate our in vitro system, we directly measured
cell volumes under different PEG concentrations and found that untreated cells
(~2600 μm³) undergo 23% volume reduction with 1% PEG (~2000 μm³) and 38%
reduction with 2% PEG (~1600 μm³). These experimental compression levels fall
34
well within the physiological range observed in vivo.
Furthermore, published in vitro reconstitution studies demonstrate that AXIN
phase separation occurs at approximately 2.5% PEG8000 (with 150 mM NaCl and
1 μM protein), confirming that our concentrations (1-2%) are at or below the
threshold required to trigger condensate formation. Importantly, our compressed
organoids maintain viability and functionality, with healthy intestinal organoids
showing enhanced growth and CRC organoids exhibiting growth inhibition without
significant cytotoxicity at 3% PEG. These data demonstrate that our PEG-
mediated compression accurately models the physiological crowding and osmotic
challenges experienced by intestinal epithelial cells in vivo.
